factual_methodology.summary: IMF Fiscal Monitor 14 October official statement; 6 October analytical chapter; EIA 6 October winter outlook; BLS August CPI and October release calendar. Release time and forecasts distinguished from observed statistics; unverified intraday prices excluded.

editorial_publication_readiness.summary: English-first and Portuguese editions reviewed for clear argument continuity, non-conversational prose, distinct evidence and inference, and final-only references. No internal publication or product roadmap material.

visual_evidence_readiness.summary: Both locales contain three comparable evidentiary tables, two signed/numeric bar charts, one causal flow, one qualitative geographic exposure map and one mechanism mindmap. Numerical chart arrays and interpretation checked for parity.

research_depth.summary: Fiscal incidence and refinancing, cross-fuel household energy expenditure heterogeneity, CPI measures and release chronology, bond-yield decomposition, conditional scenarios and falsifying evidence.

evidence_traceability.summary: Eight distinct primary-source references per locale; IMF, US BLS, and EIA official publications; original research cut off before US September CPI.

counterfactual_review.summary: Alternatives explicitly consider narrow versus broad inflation, targeted versus open-ended relief, durable versus transitory energy costs, and stable sovereign refinancing.

contrary_evidence: The EIA projects lower winter spending for households primarily using natural gas and propane; a generalised energy-bill increase is not supported.
The August core CPI increase was lower than the headline, so energy-driven inflation does not on its own establish broad price persistence.
Higher bond yields can reflect expected rates, issuance supply or term premia without demonstrating a realised solvency crisis.
Fiscal relief may be effective and sustainable when temporary, well targeted and adequately financed.
limitations: US September 2026 CPI had not been released at the research cutoff; no CPI forecast was presented as a measurement.
EIA winter bills are population-specific forecasts, not actual household expenses or weights for a national inflation index.
IMF policy recommendations are attributed to the institution, not asserted as universally optimal policy.
No October 14 intraday market prices, auctions, policy decisions or political developments were independently verified.
Editorial checking conducted in this workflow, not independent external peer review. Automated CI build and public-deployment checks are separate operational gates.
notes: Content and visual source review tied to exact Git blobs; publication conditional on unchanged sidecar and EN/PT text; keep sources at report end.

en.title: Global Macro — fiscal constraints meet uneven energy costs before the US inflation release
en.deck: The IMF's October 14 fiscal warning intersects with divergent US winter heating expenses and a still-pending September CPI release; debt refinancing and household incidence are the core transmission channels.
en.regime: Fiscal risks are elevated while the incidence of energy costs differs by household fuel, geography and financing conditions.
en.key_risk: Persistent energy costs and higher sovereign refinancing yields can constrain effective household protection.
